title: Home page redesign — fixes, Edit, look and motion

steps.path: Any card, while you use it
steps.headline: When something changes in the house, how should the page update so it stops cutting off what you are doing?
steps.today: When any light, speaker or camera changes, the page throws away every card in that area and builds them all again from scratch.
steps.problem: You are dragging a slider and it lets go. You are typing a new name in Edit and it reverts and highlights the text. A keyboard user presses a switch and loses their place. Open dropdowns close. The little slide and fade animations never play, because every card is brand new. I reproduced the slider, the typing, the keyboard focus and the video restarts.
steps.proposal: Pick how the page should refresh. All three keep the same look; they differ in how much of the page can ever be interrupted.

options.label: Protect what you are touching
options.summary: Keep rebuilding everything, but never while you are holding, typing or focused on something, and put your place back afterwards.
pros: Smallest change; the look stays exactly as it is.
Fixes drags, typing and keyboard focus quickly.
cons: Cards still blink when you are not touching them.
The slide and fade animations still never play.
Every new kind of control needs its own protection.

options.label: Change only what changed
options.summary: Each card updates itself in place: a switch slides, a number changes, the card next to it is not touched.
pros: Nothing is lost mid-use, ever: sliders, typing, focus, hover and open menus stay put.
The animations the design already has start working.
Video clips are never disturbed by an unrelated light.
cons: The biggest piece of work: every card needs its own update step.
The most chance of new bugs while it is built.

options.label: Wait for a calm moment
options.summary: Collect changes and draw them all at once when you have stopped touching the page for about a second.
pros: Fairly small change; no card is ever rebuilt under your finger.
Many quick changes become one redraw.
cons: Changes can show up a second late, for example a wall switch.
Still rebuilds every card each time it does draw, so no animations and hover resets.

steps.headline: The page redraws far more often than needed. How should it cut that down?
steps.today: A camera with a picture refreshes every 10 seconds. One press on a light redraws the page twice within a hundredth of a second. Pressing All lights in a room redraws three times. Opening the page draws camera cards three separate times.
steps.problem: In a house where nothing is changing, all cards blink about six times a minute because of the camera picture. At startup each camera card swaps from an empty grey box to a note or a list of recordings, so everything below it jumps down twice. I measured all of these.
steps.proposal: Pick how to cut the redraws.

options.label: Fix the three causes
options.summary: Keep the camera picture out of the page's text, draw once per press, and draw cameras once when they are ready.
pros: Quick, safe, obvious wins.
Quiet house stops blinking.
cons: Treats symptoms; the next feature can bring the same problem back.
Startup still shows an empty camera box first.

options.label: One drawing per moment
options.summary: Every change, from presses, the house and the checks, lands in one shared queue and the page draws once for all of them.
pros: A press is always one drawing, however many cards it touches.
Prevents this class of problem for later features.
cons: Needs care so a press still feels instant.
A moderate rewrite of how the page decides to draw.

options.label: Reserve space and draw cameras last
options.summary: Camera cards start at their final size with a quiet loading look, and are filled in without moving anything around them.
pros: Nothing jumps at startup.
Looks calmer to someone watching it load.
cons: Does not fix the repeated redraws while the page is open.
Needs a good loading look for cameras and recordings.

steps.path: Any switch or card changed outside the page
steps.headline: When the page's own check and a live update disagree, which one should win?
steps.today: The house sends changes the instant they happen, and the page also asks for everything again every minute (every 5 seconds if the live connection drops).
steps.problem: If a check is in flight when you flip the wall switch, its older answer arrives after the change and puts the card back to ON. It then stays wrong until the next check, up to a minute. Separately, if something changed while you were dragging a slider, it is not shown when you let go; it waits up to a minute. I reproduced both.

options.label: Re-apply the latest news after every check
options.summary: After a check lands, lay the newest live updates back on top, and catch up the moment you let go of a slider.
pros: Small change; fixes both cases.
Checks still find renames and new devices.
cons: Two sources of truth still exist, so a new mix-up can appear later.

options.label: The newest one wins
options.summary: Every piece of information carries when it happened, and the page keeps whichever is newer, check or live.
pros: Correct no matter what order answers arrive in.
Also covers your own presses without special cases.
cons: The check's answer carries timestamps only for some things; needs checking against the real house.
Medium-sized change.

options.label: Trust live updates, check rarely
options.summary: While the live connection works, ignore the check's device states and use it only to find renames and new devices.
pros: Simplest rule to explain.
Less data to fetch.
cons: If the live connection quietly misses an update, nothing corrects it for a long while.
Larger risk if live updates have a gap.

steps.path: Switches and sliders, when Home Assistant says no
steps.headline: When a press does not work, what should you see?
steps.today: The switch changes the instant you press it and is kept that way for 8 seconds while the house catches up. Sliders stay where you drag them.
steps.problem: If the house refuses, the switch still says ON, a red message appears and vanishes after about half a second, and 8 seconds later the switch flips back with no explanation. A slider that was refused just stays at the wrong value. I reproduced both.
steps.proposal: Pick what the page should do on a failure.

options.label: Undo straight away, keep the message
options.summary: On failure the switch or slider goes back at once and the message stays for several seconds.
pros: The page never shows something that is not true for long.
Small change.
cons: A slow device that eventually works looks briefly like a failure.

options.label: Show sending, done, failed
options.summary: The card shows a small Sending state, then settles, or shows Did not work on that card with a Try again.
pros: You always know what is happening, even for slow TVs.
The error sits on the card it is about.
cons: New wording and a new small look on every card.
More to design and test.

options.label: Shorten the wait
options.summary: Keep the instant switch but hold it for 3 seconds instead of 8, and keep the message longer.
pros: Tiny change.
A real failure is corrected faster.
cons: A slow TV may flip back and forth again, the problem the 8 seconds was added to fix.

steps.headline: How should the device pop-up behave while its information arrives and changes?
steps.today: Press and hold a card and a pop-up opens. A moment later its history arrives, and any change to that device updates it.
steps.problem: Each update rebuilds the whole pop-up. Keyboard focus drops to the page behind it, so Tab no longer stays inside; whatever you scrolled to jumps back to the top; and the pop-up grows when the history replaces Reading its history. I reproduced the focus and rebuild.
steps.proposal: Pick how the pop-up should update.

options.label: Rebuild, then put things back
options.summary: Keep rebuilding, but remember your focus and scroll position and restore them.
pros: Small change.
Fixes focus and scroll.
cons: Still blinks; still jumps in height when history arrives.

options.label: Draw it once, update the parts
options.summary: The frame and header stay; only the controls and the history list change, and the history area reserves its space.
pros: No jump, no lost focus or scroll.
Pairs naturally with A-1 Change only what changed.
cons: More work than a quick fix.
Two code paths if A-1 goes another way.

options.label: Freeze while open
options.summary: The pop-up shows what it had at opening and updates only when you press Refresh or reopen it.
pros: Rock steady.
Simple.
cons: Can show out-of-date values on a device you are actively controlling from it.

steps.headline: Should speaker ticks and new names be held steady like switches are?
steps.today: A switch you press is held in its new position until the house agrees. Ticking a speaker into a group, and renaming a device, are shown at once but not held.
steps.problem: Tick a speaker; any other update for that speaker lands before the join finishes and the tick disappears, then comes back. Reproduced. A rename can briefly show the old name in the same way (reasoned).

options.label: Hold them the same way
options.summary: Give groups and names the same short hold that switches already have.
pros: Small, consistent change.
Fixes the flip-back.
cons: Another special case to maintain.

options.label: One list of pending changes
options.summary: Every press, tick, slider and rename goes in one list; the page shows them on top of what the house says until each is confirmed or failed.
pros: One rule for everything; pairs with A-3 and A-4.
Easy to show Sending or Failed per card.
cons: The biggest change of the options.
Touches every kind of control.

options.label: Do not guess ahead
options.summary: Show a quiet Joining spinner until the house confirms.
pros: Never shows a wrong tick.
Easy to understand.
cons: Feels slower; a half-second to several seconds with nothing ticked.

steps.headline: What should happen to a playing video when the rest of the page changes, or when you leave the page?
steps.today: A recorded clip or live camera view plays inside the card. The page is rebuilt whenever something changes, and the video is taken out and put back each time.
steps.problem: A browser pauses a video the moment it is removed, so an unrelated light changing is a short stutter in a playing clip. I reproduced the remove and restart. Separately, the live view keeps drawing pictures after you switch away from the page; I read this in the code but could not run it.

options.label: Never move the video
options.summary: The card holding a video is left alone while it plays, and other cards update around it.
pros: No stutter at all.
Covered automatically if you pick Change only what changed in A-1.
cons: Needs the card to be update-in-place, or a special exception for video cards.

options.label: Pause live view when hidden
options.summary: Stop the live picture when you leave the page and show Play again when you come back.
pros: Saves battery and data.
Small change.
cons: Does not touch the clip stutter.
Live view does not resume by itself.

options.label: Stop live view after a while
options.summary: Live view stops after a couple of minutes, or when the page is left, and the clip is allowed a stutter.
pros: Simplest and cheapest.
Protects data use.
cons: A stutter while watching remains.
You may lose a view you wanted to keep.

steps.headline: Which way of editing the Home page feels simplest to you?
steps.notice: Each one starts in Edit. Star a device, hide one, rename one, move one to another room, and set a TV's sound. The pretend Home Assistant saves renames and moves. Try the tick boxes in the middle one, and drag the grips in the last one.
steps.risk: All three change how Edit looks and works; the normal page outside Edit does not change.

variants.label: Two buttons and More
variants.summary: Every card keeps its normal look, with just Favourite and Hide under it and a More button. More opens one tidy panel under that card: name, room, TV sound, earlier or later, details, and open in Home Assistant.
variants.risk: Changing many devices means opening More on each one. Rooms are still reordered with their small arrows.

variants.label: Tick, then act
variants.summary: Each card gets a Select box, and each room a Select all. Ticked cards get a bar at the bottom: favourite, hide or move them all at once. Tick just one and the bar also lets you rename it, set TV sound, reorder it, and see details.
variants.risk: The bar can cover the bottom of the page while you work, and it takes a tap to tick before anything happens.

variants.label: Organise board
variants.summary: Edit turns the page into slim rows, one line per device. Drag a row by its dots to reorder it, or into another room, or into a dashed box for a new room. Star and hide sit on each row; tap a name to open its settings.
variants.risk: You no longer see the lights and controls while editing, only names. Dragging needs a steady hand on a phone, so each row also has a Room list in its settings.

steps.headline: Which overall look should the Home page have?
steps.notice: Whichever you pick sets the feel of every card, button and tab.
steps.risk: Each one changes how everything looks, but nothing moves or works differently.

variants.label: Today
variants.summary: The page as it looks now, for comparison.

variants.label: Calm and flat
variants.summary: Room boxes disappear; devices are soft tinted tiles with a thin brightness line and round handle. Lots of air, quiet headings.
variants.risk: Less contrast between sections, so a busy house can feel a little plain.

variants.label: Glass and glow
variants.summary: Raised glass cards with soft shadows; anything that is on glows in its own colour; the open tab is filled with the theme's accent.
variants.risk: Richer but busier; glow and shadows are the most decorated of the three.

variants.label: Clean list
variants.summary: No cards: rooms are titled sections with thin dividers, devices are rows, tabs are underlined. Fits the most on screen.
variants.risk: Plainer and more document-like; devices look less tappable.

steps.headline: Which look should the device pop-up have?

steps.risk: You can mix: this does not have to match the page look you pick.

steps.notice: The list of what changed in the house today.

steps.headline: Which look should the Climate page have?
steps.notice: The thermostat dial and the weather card.
steps.risk: The weather card is the same in all three; only the surroundings change.

steps.path: Home > any tab, any card, the device pop-up
steps.headline: Which way of moving around the Home page feels most polished without slowing you down?
steps.notice: Do the same in each: click Lights, Media, Home, then the gear. In Destin's Room open and close the Lights arrow, Scenes, the TV's Remote and a speaker's Group. Press and hold a card (or right-click) for the pop-up; close it with X, Escape, then a click outside. Click quickly between things.
steps.risk: All three add a short movement (about a fifth of a second) to actions that are instant today. None of them moves anything when the page refreshes by itself, and all turn off if the computer is set to reduce motion.

variants.label: Quiet fades
variants.summary: What you open fades in and rises a few pixels. The page you leave does not move. Closing a card fades its contents out first; closing the pop-up fades it away. The arrows turn smoothly.
variants.risk: The calmest, but cards below a card you open or close still jump to their new places, and closing a card waits about a tenth of a second before it happens.

variants.label: Whole-page morph
variants.summary: The browser takes a snapshot before and after each click and blends between them. Room cards slide and stretch to their new size, the tab row stays put, and the pop-up fades up from slightly smaller.
variants.risk: Touches the most screen at once, and during the short blend (a fifth of a second) the page ignores clicks. Text inside a stretching card can look briefly squashed. Costs the most on a slow computer.

variants.label: Glide and grow
variants.summary: Pages slide in from the side the tab sits on, and the filled tab glides along the row. The pop-up grows out of the card you pressed and shrinks back into it. A card's contents drop in one after another, and cards below glide to their new places.
variants.risk: The most movement, so the most noticeable. The pop-up's text looks stretched for the first moment while it grows, and a card that opens near the screen's edge can make the glide look uneven.

steps.path: Home > a room's lights and TV
steps.headline: When you switch lights and TVs on and off, which one feels the most acknowledged and alive?
steps.notice: In Destin's Room press a light's round bulb to turn it off and on. Press the room's All tile. Press the TV's power button. Drag a brightness bar slowly, then pick another colour under a light. The small "Try" strip at the bottom of each pane is only for this test and will not be in the real page.
steps.risk: Motion plays only on the card you pressed. If the page redraws while it plays, it carries on from where it was instead of restarting.

variants.label: Settle
variants.summary: Every change eases in quietly: the glow fades up and the bulb gives one small pop, the playing block rises into place, a thermostat number slides, and a change from elsewhere gets one soft outline that fades.
variants.risk: Quietest: on and off may feel almost too subtle if you want the page to feel dramatic.

variants.label: Acknowledge and wait
variants.summary: Built for slow devices: a ripple appears under your finger at once, a thin bar runs along the card until the device answers, then a green tick shows. A change from elsewhere gets a small "Just changed" label. Dragging shows the number above the handle.
variants.risk: Switching itself is plain; the feel comes from the ripple and the waiting bar, which only show up while the device is slow.

variants.label: Spread and spring
variants.summary: The most lively: light spreads out from the bulb across the card, the bulb springs, and a room's All makes its lights switch one after another. The playing block unfolds, the play button spins in, and a change from elsewhere gets a passing shine.
variants.risk: Switching a whole room plays several effects at once, which some people find busy. Needs a small extra step to keep the effects from being cut off.

steps.headline: When music, speakers, the thermostat or a camera change, which one shows it best without getting in your way?
steps.notice: On the Living Room speaker press play, then next, then mute. Open its Group list and tick another speaker. On the Thermostat press the + and - buttons. On a camera press Watch live if it offers it. The small "Try" strip at the bottom of each pane is only for this test and will not be in the real page.
steps.risk: The playing block appears by a layout jump in all three; the options only change how it looks arriving, not where things sit.

variants.label: Settle
variants.summary: Every change eases in quietly: the glow fades up and the bulb gives one small pop, the playing block rises into place, a thermostat number slides, and a change from elsewhere gets one soft outline that fades.
variants.risk: The thermostat number slides a little; nothing else reacts to a temperature change.

variants.label: Acknowledge and wait
variants.summary: Built for slow devices: a ripple appears under your finger at once, a thin bar runs along the card until the device answers, then a green tick shows. A change from elsewhere gets a small "Just changed" label. Dragging shows the number above the handle.
variants.risk: Controls give a ripple at once but the playing block simply appears.

variants.label: Spread and spring
variants.summary: The most lively: light spreads out from the bulb across the card, the bulb springs, and a room's All makes its lights switch one after another. The playing block unfolds, the play button spins in, and a change from elsewhere gets a passing shine.
variants.risk: Springs and spins on small buttons can feel playful; on a phone they add to what is happening on a small screen.

steps.path: Home, slow devices and changes made elsewhere
steps.headline: When a device is slow, or someone changes something elsewhere, which one tells you best what is going on?
steps.notice: Press Slow device so it says ON, then press a light: see what the card does for three seconds. Turn it off. Press Flip a lamp from elsewhere and watch the Destin's Room lights (it can take up to five seconds to arrive). Press Replay first load to see loading. The small "Try" strip at the bottom of each pane is only for this test and will not be in the real page.
steps.risk: The waiting bar and tick are shown only while a press is waiting for the device; a device that never answers shows the bar for up to nine seconds, then nothing.

variants.label: Settle
variants.summary: Every change eases in quietly: the glow fades up and the bulb gives one small pop, the playing block rises into place, a thermostat number slides, and a change from elsewhere gets one soft outline that fades.
variants.risk: While waiting, nothing shows that the device has not answered yet; the card just looks done.
